Hello,

Thanks for the advice re: upgrade. I would definitely appreciate any pointers in terms of debugging. I took to some time to comment my code (for the model + toy data).

I am new to rstan so have done this in baby steps.

The one I one having trouble with in the zero inflated ordinal probit with correlated errors model (ZIOPC) but have attached the models that led up to it in case they help.  The zero inflated ordered logit model is the most straightforward adaptation of the ZI poisson model found on page 299 of the rstan version 1.3 reference. (I say "straightforward" since it can use the ordered_logistic function). The ZIOP model works sometimes (depending on starting values).

By way of background on the model, zero inflation occurs in discrete models when there is an excess of zeros. For example, in count models, if the outbreak of wars between two countries follows a poisson distribution, there will be an excess of zeros from countries that would never consider fighting one another (like the US vs Canada in all contexts apart from the Southpark movie). Or, if you have a Likert scale asking people how much they smoke, a large group of might never smoke at all, biasing estimates of what makes people smoke "a lot" vis-a-vis "sometimes." This can be measured as mixture of two latent processes - an initial binary decision (to smoke) and an ordinal decision (how much). (This is the worked empirical example from Harris and Zhao's 2007 Journal of Econometrics paper on zero inflated ordinal models.)  Now, usually, there is no difference between ordinal probit and ordinal logit, but in this case there is. Suppose you believe that error terms between the two latent pieces of the model to be correlated. For example, you believe parental smoking influences both whether or not respondents would ever smoke, and, if so, how much they would smoke, but are concerned that there is some measurement error on parental smoking that would manifest in both places. If the ordinal outcome is modeled as a bivariate normal, the correlation between errors of the two structural equations can be modeled. (But it is not clear how to do this with the logit model.)  
 
So, the most immediate problem is that once I introduce transformed parameters, rstan seems to confuse terms like "real," "vector," and "matrix" for variable names. My other question is whether I have used the bivariate normal functions correctly -- what I need is the CDF, the bivariate equivalent of Phi(), and hope that I am incrementing the log probability correctly based on that. Other than that, I know that I have a lot to do on these models, but any questions or comments are more than welcome!!

I'm not new to Stan and I still do this for every model
I build. I even went so far as to write an intro chapter
in the manual recommending ing this strategy.
> The one I one having trouble with in the zero inflated ordinal probit with correlated errors model (ZIOPC) but have

> straightforward adaptation of the ZI poisson model found on page 299 of the rstan version 1.3 reference. (I say
> "straightforward" since it can use the ordered_logistic function). The ZIOP model works sometimes (depending on starting
> values).

Some models are too much for Stan to initialize and
converge (for reasons relating to both
arithmetic precision and the behavior in tails of
distributions).

Are there some reasonable initial points (ideally with
some jitter) that you can use?

> In case anyone reading this is not familiar with these models, zero inflation occurs in categorical models when there is

> an excess of zeros. For example, in count models, if the outbreak of wars between two countries follows a poisson
> distribution, there will be an excess of zeros from countries that would never consider fighting one another (like the
> US vs Canada in all contexts apart from the Southpark movie). Or, if you have a Likert scale asking people how much they
> smoke, a large group of might never smoke at all, biasing estimates of what makes people smoke "a lot" vis-a-vis
> "sometimes." This can be measured as mixture of two latent processes - an initial binary decision (to smoke) and an
> ordinal decision (how much). (This is the worked empirical example from Harris and Zhao's 2007 Journal of Econometrics
> paper on zero inflated ordinal models.) Now, usually, there is no difference between ordinal probit and ordinal logit,
> but in this case there is.

And in case anyone doesn't see how this can be implemented in
Stan, the key idea is that it follows the mixture model definition.

Because we don't have discrete parameters, you
have to marginalize out the mixture indicator; there's an example
for the zero-inflated Poisson in the appendix on comparing BUGS to Stan.

> Suppose you believe that error terms between the two latent pieces of the model to be
> correlated. For example, you believe parental smoking influences both whether or not respondents would ever smoke, and,
> if so, how much they would smoke, but are concerned that there is some measurement error on parental smoking that would
> manifest in both places. If the ordinal outcome is modeled as a bivariate normal, the correlation between the two
> structural equations can be modeled. (But it is not clear how to do this with the logit model.)
There's a multivariate logistic distribution, too.

> So, the most immediate problem is that once I introduce transformed parameters, rstan seems to confuse terms like
> "real," "vector," and "matrix" for variable names.
What do you mean by

> My other question is whether I have used the bivariate normal
> functions correctly -- what I need is the CDF, the bivariate equivalent of Phi(), and hope that I am incrementing the
> log probability correctly based on that.

We don't have a bivariate CDF function. So you'd have
to define it yourself. There's already a feature request for it,
so it's on the to-do list.

- Bob

Il 21/10/2013 20:47, pete mohanty ha scritto:
> I have reattached that file as a .txt file.

May I?

for (n in 1:N) {
zeros[n] ~ bernoulli(Phi(-gamma*z[n]));
vector[2] eta;
...

Declarations such as "vector[2] eta;" must come before statements.
After a (sampling) statement such as "zeros[n] ~ etc.", Stan looks for
another statement or a closing brace. This is why you get:

variable "vector" does not exist.
Parser expecting: "}"

lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log(normal_cdf(-gamma*z[n], 0, 1)),
log(normal_cdf(gamma*z[n], 0, 1)) + multi_normal_log(eta, mu, sigma);

A closing ")" is missing.

eta <- x[n]*beta - c[k-1];
theta[k] <- exp(multi_normal_log(eta, mu, sigma));
eta <- x[n]*beta - c[k];

eta is a vector, x[n]*beta - c[...] are scalar. You can't assign a
scalar to a vector.
eta[<1 or 2>] <- x[n]*beta - c[...] would work.

# theta[K] <- exp(multi_normal_log(eta, mu, possigma));
theta[k] <- 1 - sum(theta[1:(K-1)]);

You are outside the for (k in 2:(K-1)) loop, so "k" does not exist.

HTH

Sergio
